results.title: Profiles In History: Autograph Auction 34 Fall 2002
results.creator: Profiles in History
results.description: Profiles in History: Autograph Auction 34 Winter 2002 Auction Highlights include: Erwin Rommel's raw, triumphant postcard sent on the literal opening week of WWII. Harry Truman's unedited reflections on brawling with Stalin and Churchill at Potsdam. Daniel Boone's hand-drawn Kentucky boundary logs. FDR's localized 1927 ballot where he hand-wrote Eleanor Roosevelt into local office. Presidential & Foundational Era John Adams (December 10, 1799): An exceptionally rare official letter signed as President to the U.S. Senate. Adams explicitly praises the promptitude and zeal of federal troops used to crush the Fries Rebellion in eastern Pennsylvania. The catalog highlights a fascinating backstory: local farmers revolted over direct property taxes passed to fund defense against France. While Adams declared the riot a "highhanded" dangerous affair, he determined it wasn't treason and eventually issued a full pardon—a move that cost him critical support from his own conservative Federalist Party during the tight election of 1800. John Quincy Adams (June 6, 1791): A rare early autograph letter signed to a legal colleague named "Putnam". Written right after his admission to the bar, Adams coordinates a legal writ before playfully adding that the intricate question posed to him is too perplexing for a busy day, proposing they instead discuss it soon over "a segar [cigar] & glass of wine". John Quincy Adams Stock Certificate (April 17, 1809): An original stock certificate for the Boylston Market Association, signed by Adams as its very first president. The historic market complex was built far out of town at the time and named after Adams' second cousin, Ward Nicholas Boylston. James Bowdoin (March 30, 1786): An important Revolutionary War-era letter signed as Governor of Massachusetts to the Governor of North Carolina. Bowdoin officially states that Massachusetts has acceded to Virginia's proposal to hold the Annapolis Convention in Maryland to regulate interstate trade. This meeting ultimately served as the critical precursor to the 1787 Philadelphia Convention, where the weak Articles of Confederation were discarded in favor of the U.S. Constitution. James Buchanan (March 13, 1859): An exceptional pre-Civil War letter signed as President to Indian Affairs Commissioner James Denver. Buchanan voices deep gratitude for Denver's firm, impartial leadership as the territorial Governor of Kansas during the incredibly violent "Bleeding Kansas" border wars. Millard Fillmore (September 15, 1869): A handwritten letter showing a warm kinship between two U.S. presidents. Fillmore writes to voice his deep relief that the newly inaugurated Chief Executive, Ulysses S. Grant, had returned home safely and was on the path to recovering his health after an unexpected illness forced him to miss the New York State Fair. James A. Garfield (April 15, 1881): An exceptionally rare official letter of state signed as President. Garfield authorizes the Secretary of State to affix the Seal of the United States to his formal reply to a congratulatory message from the Republic of San Marino. Because Garfield was tragically shot by an assassin just two and a half months later, documents signed during his brief 6-month presidency are of immense rarity. James A. Garfield on Lincoln's Funeral (May 2, 1865): A poignant handwritten letter written as a Representative from Ohio to Speaker of the House Schuyler Colfax. Garfield writes from his home state to describe traveling to Cleveland to meet Abraham Lincoln’s slow-moving funeral train. He expresses deep regret that Colfax was unable to accompany the cortege, creating an incredible historical link between the first and second U.S. presidents to be assassinated. Andrew Jackson Walking Cane Letter (c. January/February 1831): An exceptional letter signed as President to a Virginia resident, typed out by his adopted son. Jackson warmly accepts a presentation walking cane carved from a tree that stood on the physical battlefield of the Battle of New Orleans. Jackson praises the brave men whose valor served as the "Security of the Union," referencing the legendary War of 1812 victory that vaulted his military persona into the White House. Andrew Jackson Land Grant (January 1, 1830): A document signed as President on vellum, granting a 113-acre plot of land located near St. Louis, Missouri. Thomas Jefferson & the UVA Rotunda (October 7, 1823): A magnificent autograph letter signed from Monticello to Master Carpenter James Oldham. Writing as the "Father of the University of Virginia," the aging former president outlines the ongoing construction of the university's famous architectural crown jewel, the UVA Rotunda. Jefferson rejects Oldham’s direct financial appeals to the Board of Visitors regarding a wage dispute, telling him that contractual adjustments must go through the executive proctor or the ordinary courts. This exact letter famously triggered the very first lawsuit brought against the University of Virginia. Thomas Jefferson Navy Commission (March 16, 1807): An exceptional document signed as President (countersigned by Navy Secretary Robert Smith) commissioning Hethcote J. Reed as a Lieutenant. Reed served as a midshipman on the historic frigate USS Constitution ("Old Ironsides") during the Barbary Coast patrols and fought in the celebrated assault on Tripoli during the Tripolitan War. Thomas Jefferson & James Madison Ships' Papers (December 30, 1806): A large folio-sized safe-passage document signed jointly by Jefferson as President and Madison as Secretary of State. The document features a rare four-language parallel text configuration (English, Dutch, French, and Spanish) granting passage to a brig carrying livestock and lumber out of an American port. William Henry Harrison Political Overtures (July 12, 1837): A dense, 4-page political strategy letter written to Whig organizer Silas M. Stilwell. Harrison plots with party allies Daniel Webster and Henry Clay to overthrow the Jacksonian Democrats in the upcoming 1840 election. Harrison warns his party to respect their opponents' perfect discipline, delivering a timeless political axiom: "Confidence in the weakness of our enemy has produced the most disastrous defeats on record." John F. Kennedy Handwritten Note (January 10, 1962): An incredibly rare autograph letter signed as President on official green White House stationery. Writing to a former Senate colleague ("Senator Martin"), Kennedy sends friendly New Year's greetings, marking one of only a handful of full one-page handwritten presidential letters from JFK in private hands. Herbert Hoover Signed Portrait (Undated): A handsome sepia portrait photograph of the smartly dressed president, warmly inscribed to a local doctor. Herbert Hoover anti-FDR Rant (September 3, 1934): A scathing 2-page typed letter attacking the newly formed "American Liberty League". Hoover accuses the disgruntled corporate Democrats backing the league of hijacking the 1932 Republican platform, bluntly declaring that he has no more confidence in their Wall Street model of liberty than the New Deal model. Herbert Hoover Teapot Dome Speech (November 14, 1933): A signed 5-page transcript of the speech Hoover delivered at the dedication of the Warren G. Harding Memorial. Hoover fiercely castigates the corrupt Teapot Dome conspirators for violating public trust. Historically, Teapot Dome ringleader Harry M. Daugherty sat seething barely thirty feet away in the audience as Hoover spoke. James Madison War-Date Letter (January 5, 1813): A superb presidential letter written marked "private" to his newly elected Vice President, Elbridge Gerry. Madison answers technical questions regarding taking the constitutional oath of office. He urges the aging Gerry to travel south to Virginia to avoid the harsh winter weather, writing: "Your friends in Virginia will then be the gainers..." The catalog highlights that Gerry followed Madison's advice and took his oath at home in Cambridge before taking his seat as president pro tempore of the Senate. This letter is also famous for detailing the origin of the term "gerrymander," coined after Gerry distorted Massachusetts voting districts to look like a salamander. James Madison Cabinet Strife Letter (August 29, 1810): A fascinating autograph letter signed as President to his bitter political rival, Senator Samuel Smith. Madison handles tense complaints regarding Treasury deposits and defends his embattled Treasury Secretary, Albert Gallatin. This letter captures a highly unstable moment in Madison's administration, balancing a divided cabinet alongside a deteriorating relationship with Napoleon on the brink of the War of 1812. James Madison Ship's Passport (June 1, 1811): A scallop-top ship's passport signed on vellum by President Madison, countersigned by Secretary of State Robert Smith, granting safe passage to a two-gun schooner named the Fly of Bristol. James K. Polk Grandfather Vindication (August 24, 1844): A handwritten campaign letter marked "Private" to a Nashville editor. Polk fiercely defends against toxic Whig character attacks that accused his grandfather, Col. Ezekiel Polk, of being a Revolutionary War Tory (a British loyalist). Polk biography notes that Polk became entirely obsessed with this issue, spending more energy defending his grandfather's memory than almost any other topic in the tight 1844 election. Franklin D. Roosevelt Scripture Beliefs (January 6, 1929): A typed letter written as Governor of New York to a Texas reverend, explicitly confirming his deep reliance on the Bible: "Please understand that I read the Scriptures and believe in the Book from cover to cover, and am trying to carry out the teaching of the Master as best I can." Franklin D. Roosevelt Disabled Veterans Message (December 24, 1935): A moving typed letter signed as President, delivered on Christmas Eve to a World War I veterans organization. Roosevelt praises the noble living and noble dead, offering the everlasting gratitude of the nation they served. Franklin D. Roosevelt Dutchess County Absentee Ballot (November 8, 1927): An extraordinary legal voting archive completed and signed three times by FDR just before his election as Governor of New York. Voting an all-Democrat ticket, Roosevelt casts a vote against the extension of the New York Governor's term (a historic irony given he would later break all boundaries by winning four terms as President). Best of all, on the local town section, Roosevelt explicitly hand-writes in his wife, Eleanor Roosevelt, as School Director for Hyde Park. Eleanor Roosevelt on Joseph P. Kennedy (June 21): A rare handwritten letter signed as First Lady to her son James. Eleanor recounts hosting a porch picnic lunch for the Kennedy family patriarch, Joseph P. Kennedy, leaving a sharp and incredibly shrewd historical assessment of the future ambassador: "Joe Kennedy has been here... I enjoyed listening to him. A complete egotist but an intelligent & kindly one." Harry S. Truman on Potsdam & McCarthy (May 28, 1954): A spectacular 6-page autograph letter signed "Harry" to his former Secretary of State, Dean Acheson. Truman recounts working on his memoirs 17 hours a day and relives an exasperated clash he had at the Potsdam Conference with Winston Churchill and Joseph Stalin regarding Spanish dictator Francisco Franco. He tells Acheson that he snapped at the dictators, declaring he didn't come to Berlin to run a "police court". When translated, Stalin roared with laughter and suggested they talk about Poland instead. Truman then transitions to domestic affairs, bluntly observing that the ongoing Sen. Joseph McCarthy anti-communist hearings are causing massive shame to his Republican friends. He sharply criticizes the Eisenhower White House as "smart but inexperienced boys" who are upsetting NATO and throwing away America's military strength while dangerously eyeing intervention in Indo-China. Harry S. Truman on JFK & the 1960 Convention (July 9, 1960): Another remarkable handwritten letter signed "Harry" to Dean Acheson, penned just two days before the 1960 Democratic National Convention. Truman writes that party leaders are begging him to attend, adding that he intends to "have a lot of fun with the guessers and the prophets." The catalog notes that Truman strongly disliked John F. Kennedy, previously calling him too inexperienced and publicly demanding: "Senator, are you certain that you are quite ready for the country?" Woodrow Wilson on the British Blockade (March 19, 1915): A typed letter signed as President, accompanied by a hand-corrected 4-page Letter of State addressed to Great Britain regarding their aggressive naval blockade off Germany. Wilson warns the British government that their unusually massive shipping cordon violates international law by burdening neutral American merchantmen. This warning was terrifyingly on-point: just two weeks later, the German navy retaliated against the blockade zone, sinking the passenger liner Lusitania and drowning nearly 200 Americans. Woodrow Wilson Literature Quote (October 16, 1899): A beautiful, signed autograph quote penned while serving as the President of Princeton University: "Literature is a thing of convictions, of insights, of what is felt and seen and heard and hoped for."Zachary Taylor (June 19, 1850): An incredibly rare letter signed as President, written to New York Governor Hamilton Fish less than one month before Taylor's sudden death in office. Taylor declines an invitation to the New York State Fair, noting that he cannot leave Washington while Congress is aggressively debating the highly controversial Compromise of 1850 regarding the extension of slavery. Taylor fell ill five days after July 4th and passed away from rampaging cholera. William H. Taft on the League of Nations (December 18, 1920): A typed letter signed regarding a controversy over the omission of any reference to God in the preamble to the League of Nations' charter. Taft notes he would have strongly favored a recognition of the Deity, but argues that the omission wasn't sinister and doesn't justify a big debate, concluding: "Preambles are not the substance of the League, and it is about the substance that we are interested." Civil War, Military, & Global Affairs Jefferson Davis (March 20, 1863): A high-stakes Civil War-date letter signed as President of the C.S.A. to Georgia Governor J.E. Brown. Davis addresses a tense military incident where Confederate General Braxton Bragg ordered his quartermasters to use armed force, if necessary, to seize control of Georgia's state-owned Western & Atlantic Railroad after transit workers allegedly refused to transport Southern munitions. Davis acts as an urgent diplomat, regretting the general's extra-legal threats and smoothing over state-versus-federal tensions with a plea for Southern solidarity. Turner Ashby (February 29, 1862): A highly scarce Confederate army receipt signed by Ashby as Colonel in Winchester, Virginia, securing transport wagons and horses. Ashby was one of "Stonewall" Jackson's most trusted cavalry subordinates and was tragically killed in action just three months later. Ellis Spear of the 20th Maine (Undated): A fascinating 5-page original autograph manuscript recounting the close-quarters horrors of the 1864 Wilderness Campaign and the Battle of Spotsylvania Court House. Spear, who took command of the legendary regiment after Joshua Chamberlain was promoted, reflects on the exhausting night marches and constant skirmishes that were enough to make a veteran tired just thinking about it decades later. Joshua L. Chamberlain & Thomas D. Chamberlain (October 12, 1870): A unique historical check filled out by the "Savior of Gettysburg" and signed jointly by both famous brothers. Thomas served as a captain under Joshua, and famously survived a near-fatal close-range gun encounter while successfully securing the Union's left flank on Little Round Top. William F. Smith (March 11, 1891): A candid post-war letter where the former Union Major General admits he is writing a defense paper to evaluate the battlefield performance of General Grant. Smith controversially concludes that General Grant was a poor military commander compared to Confederate generals, echoing a highly unpopular public opinion at the time. Edward Townsend (March 30, 1865): An official State Department invitation presented to the Governor of Missouri to witness the historic flag-raising ceremony at Fort Sumter. Scheduled for April 14, 1865—exactly four years to the day after the fort fell—the event allowed General Robert Anderson to re-raise the very same tattered garrison flag that had marked the literal start of the Civil War. David Ben-Gurion (March 13, 1954): A powerful letter handwritten in Hebrew from his retreat in Sde Boker to a Knesset member. Ben-Gurion issues a stark warning to "naive" pacifists, declaring that Israel must rid itself of illusions that external Jewish organizations can guarantee safety from border raids, fiercely arguing that the sole security of Israel lies with the IDF. Catherine the Great (January 9, 1793): A beautiful, tender New Year's greeting letter written in French by the Russian Empress to her sister, the Princess of Anhalt-Zerbst. Abraham Lincoln Legal Opinion (August 17, 1850): A full-page autograph letter signed from Springfield, Illinois, regarding a civil land title dispute. Evaluating a forged property deed, Lincoln delivers a characteristically blunt and succinct legal assessment: "This is the whole story — The case can not be gained by much talking." Abraham Lincoln Circuit Court Receipt (May 1, 1858): A handwritten financial document signed as an Illinois general practice attorney. Dated just six weeks before his famous "House Divided" speech propelled him to national visibility, Lincoln signs off on court fees received for a case in the Vermilion Circuit Court. Robert E. Lee Lexington Correspondence (June 22, 1866): A gracious 2-page letter written as President of Washington College to a former Union soldier, Major Richard P. Hammond. Writing just one year after the war ended, Lee attempts to track down a missing Confederate general on behalf of his former battlefield adversary, showcasing the smooth, respectful resumption of peace between North and South. Robert E. Lee Signature (March 8, 1869): A bold, clean ink signature reading "R.E. Lee," clipped from a larger document. John Hancock Military Appointment (July 1, 1775): A spectacular Revolutionary War document signed boldly by Hancock as President of the Continental Congress, countersigned by Charles Thomson. Hancock appoints an ensign to the Massachusetts Regiment just two weeks after the bloody Battle of Bunker Hill, and a mere two days before George Washington arrived in Cambridge to assume formal command of the Continental Army. Julia Ward Howe Battle Hymn of the Republic Manuscript (March 21, 1865): A monumental piece of American cultural history. A complete 2-page autograph manuscript of her famous Union rallying anthem, written entirely in her hand and signed just two weeks before Robert E. Lee's surrender at Appomattox. Incredibly, this specific copy features an un-published extra stanza attacking god's contemners that did not make it into the final Atlantic Monthly printing. Francis Gary Powers U-2 Spy Flight Letter (September 22, 1970): A rare typed letter signed by the famous Cold War pilot to an aviation magazine editor. Powers reviews a book tracking the history of aerial reconnaissance, commenting on the super-secret CIA U-2 program that caused an international crisis when he was shot down over downtown Moscow in 1960. Theodor Herzl Zionist Letter (August 10, 1902): A printed political letter signed by the zionist leader from Vienna. Written right as critical negotiations with the Ottoman Empire collapsed, Herzl outlines the upcoming agenda for the Zionist Action Committee, which marked his historic shift to lobby the British government for a Jewish homeland. Nathaniel Lyon Pre-Battle Report (May 12, 1861): An exceptionally rare Civil War letter written from the St. Louis Arsenal just three months before Lyon was killed in action. Writing to the Adjutant General, Lyon reports on a local clash where Union troops and a civilian mob engaged in a deadly shootout, killing 12 people. Lyon openly criticizes his brash superior, General William S. Harney, warning that Harney's erratic city orders painfully embarrass his covert strategy to stop pro-Confederate combinations from seizing the state of Missouri. Philip H. Sheridan Legendary War Horse Letter (March 24, 1876): A wonderful letter penned by the Union hero to an old army comrade. Sheridan reveals that the famous black horse he rode during his frantic, morale-boosting race from Winchester to rally his routed troops at the Battle of Cedar Creek is still alive and well in his possession, noting: "He looks almost as well now as when you saw him in Virginia." Sheridan later renamed the black horse "Winchester." George H. Thomas on the Fitz John Porter Court-Martial (January 5, 1870): An autograph letter signed by the Union general known as "The Rock of Chickamauga." Thomas comments on the infamous Civil War court-martial of Gen. Fitz John Porter, who was relieved of command for alleged dereliction of duty during the Battle of Groveton. Thomas defends Porter's character, stating he never believed Porter willfully neglected his duty. George Washington Free Frank (Undated): A prominent, large ink signature reading "Go: Washington," scrawled as a free-franked address panel to a Connecticut cobbler named Joseph Webb. Historical records indicate Washington wrote to Webb primarily to check on custom orders for "horse skin" boots. George Washington on Long Island Plundering (October 31, 1778): A superb Revolutionary War-date letter signed by the Commander-in-Chief from his headquarters in Fredericksburg. Washington issues a stern reprimand to a local major after learning that Continental scouts traveling to Long Island under the pretext of gathering intelligence were indiscriminately plundering and distressing the local inhabitants. Washington commands him to stop the pernicious practice, explicitly ordering him to only employ those as spies or observers in whom he can place proper confidence. Daniel Boone Fayette County Survey (May 15, 1785): A mind-bogglingly rare complete manuscript document written and signed by the legendary pioneer as a Deputy Surveyor in Fayette County, Kentucky. Boone hand-writes the boundary logs for a 1,000-acre land plot using uncorrected frontier misspellings, tracing lines from "2 Shuger trees" to a "white oke and hickory." Boone tragically lost almost all of his own land in this exact county three years later due to title disputes. Simon Kenton Frontier Warrant (Undated): A financial document signed by the famous trans-Allegheny frontiersman who famously saved Daniel Boone's life during an Indian raid at Boonesborough. Science, Discovery, & Literature Benjamin Franklin (April 9, 1773): A magnificent 2-page autograph letter signed and initialed from London to "Dear Jenky" (Jane Parker). Franklin musters his immense powers of diplomacy to resolve a delicate financial disagreement with the family of his deceased New York printing business partner. To preserve their long family tie, Franklin delivers a timeless piece of advice: "But I think it contributes to the Duration of Friendship to keep its Accounts, & those of Business distinct & separate; and that an exact Justice in Pounds Shillings & Pence should be observed between Friends as between Strangers." Albert Einstein "World State" Manuscript (Undated, Post-WWI): A monumental 3-page unsigned autograph manuscript written in green ink. Einstein maps out a bold political plan for a unified "World State", arguing that the League of Nations failed because member states refused to surrender their individual sovereignty. He argues that a global political system is unconditionally necessary to stop our planet from becoming unbearable for humans, while warning that intellectuals often fail in politics because they lack quick decision-making and human people skills. Tantalizingly, the top of the page features a series of Einstein's handwritten mathematical equations in electromagnetics. Albert Einstein Signed Portrait (1935): A classic black-and-white portrait of Einstein in a tuxedo, beautifully inscribed in German to friends in remembrance of "happy musical evenings" spent playing his beloved violin. John Flamsteed (June 29, 1695): A rare signed financial receipt from the historic first Astronomer Royal of England. Flamsteed's meticulous star mapping directly provided the data Sir Isaac Newton used to verify his legendary theory of gravity. Raymond Chandler (November 5, 1946): A typed letter to his famous Hollywood agent, H.N. Swanson. Written right as Chandler abandoned the stress of the movie studios for the quiet coast of La Jolla, he tracks short story publishing rights while jokingly describing himself as "a guy who never says one thing when four will do." Samuel Francis Smith (December 4, 1893): A wonderful letter from the composer of "My Country, 'Tis of Thee", hoping his anthem kindles a spirit of freedom worldwide. Smith shares a lively reflection on aging, quoting Oliver Wendell Holmes Sr.'s birthday tribute to fellow hymn-writer Julia Ward Howe, noting that the human spirit can burn in perpetual youth if kept active. Herman Melville Defending Mardi (June 5, 1849): A magnificent 3-page autograph letter signed to his British publisher Richard Bentley (who would publish Moby-Dick two years later). Melville defends his new novel Mardi, which British critics had violently panned as too abstract and metaphysical, writing a timeless defense of the artist's mind: "But some of us scribblers, my Dear Sir, always have a certain something unmanageable in us, that bids us do this or that, and be done it must – hit or miss." He then reveals he is shifting ground away from the South Seas to write a plain, straightforward, amusing sea narrative with no metaphysics—his semi-autobiographical masterpiece, Redburn: His First Voyage. Melville letters are of legendary rarity. Claude Monet London Illness (March 14, 1901): A poignant 5-page letter handwritten in French on Savoy Hotel stationery to his wife. Monet gripes about a sudden illness that struck him down in London just as he was attempting one last creative effort to capture the Gothic spires of Westminster rising through the changing Thames fog, producing his legendary London Series of impressionist masterpieces. Franklin D. Roosevelt Founding the March of Dimes (April 7, 1927): A historic handwritten letter signed on legal stationery regarding the incorporation of the Georgia Warm Springs Foundation (later known nationwide as the March of Dimes). Paralyzed by polio, FDR details establishing the foundation as a non-profit rehabilitation center to help fellow polio victims find strength, creating one of his most enduring humanitarian health legacies. Jack London on The Call of the Wild (August 28, 1903): A mind-bogglingly rare autograph letter written in pencil to an early reader immediately following the publication of his masterpiece. London explains his creative structure for the novel, revealing his logic behind naming his legendary canine protagonist: "The only reason I named him Buck was that years before I had filed away among my notes as appropriate dog names ‘Buck’ & ‘Bright.’ ... I chose Buck – I guess because it was stronger than Bright." He beautifully adds: "We know little or nothing about what dogs think. But then we may conclude from their actions what their mental processes might be..." West Africa Slave Trade Uprising (January 15, 1808): A terrifying historical letter written by two slave traders aboard the Ship Hibernia near the St. Paul's River in Sierra Leone. Writing at the absolute peak of the Atlantic slave trade, they describe a massive, violent slave uprising where hundreds of local fighters descended upon their factory staging fort, plundering the stores, cutting the trader's hand, and forcing them to flee under cover of night. Letters detailing slave trade mutinies written directly from Africa are of immense historical scarcity. Hollywood, Sports, & Pop Culture Dwight D. Eisenhower (November 22, 1944): A deeply moving wartime letter written from Versailles to his wife, Mamie. The Supreme Allied Commander handles regular family business—enclosing $25 to help buy a durable Christmas gift for their son—before offering a somber look at the front lines: "Well sweet I’d like to think that this mess would be over soon... But the fighting and the dying go on – and the end is not yet. ‘Civilization’ is not pretty, when it resorts to war." Josephine Earp (March 3, 1929): An incredibly rare autograph letter signed by the wife of legendary gunfighter Wyatt Earp. Written just months after Wyatt's death, the former actress coordinates travel details while defending her late husband's untamed frontier legacy. Thomas Edison on Theodore Roosevelt (April 1919): An original autograph note scrawled on a poem written by a 13-year-old girl honoring the late President. Edison writes in pencil: "Some Girl! It’s in the blood capacity for high mental action accompanies the germ plasm..." 1951 Brooklyn Dodgers Signed Baseball: An official ball signed by 22 legendary members of the team, including Chuck Dressen, Gil Hodges, Pee Wee Reese, and Jackie Robinson. This historic ball dates to the exact, infamous season that culminated in Ralph Branca giving up the pennant-winning "Shot Heard 'Round the World" home run to the rival Giants. Ty Cobb Batting Advice Letter (September 14, 1954): A massive 5-page strategy letter written in green ink by "The Georgia Peach" to Pirates manager Fred Haney. Cobb offers dense, un-asked-for advice to pull a struggling hitter out of a slump, detailing exact hand placements, swinging parallels, and a warning to stop swinging for the fences. Cooperstown Hall of Fame Signed Bat: An official souvenir baseball bat signed boldly on the barrel by 13 legendary titans, including Ted Williams, Mickey Mantle, Willie Mays, Hank Aaron, and a highly controversial addition by Pete Rose. Irving Berlin Signed Sheet Music (1938): Vintage sheet music for "Alexander's Ragtime Band", beautifully inscribed by Berlin to fellow Academy Award-nominated Hollywood film composer Lew Pollack. Lucille Ball (Undated): A gorgeous sepia publicity photograph featuring her resting elegantly on a ship's helm, signed with warm sentiments. Josephine Baker (1935): A spectacular, oversized vintage photograph of the exotic stage dancer captured mid-performance, signed with a bold French inscription. P.T. Barnum (November 30, 1887): A beautiful letter written to a young boy, where the legendary showman lovingly promises that his traveling circus, "The Greatest Show on Earth", will be even larger, funnier, and more marvelous next year. George Gershwin An American in Paris Photograph (March 1929): An extraordinary sepia portrait showing the legendary composer seated at his piano. In the lower margin, Gershwin beautifully pens an autograph musical quotation consisting of four bars of music, mapping out the famous primary orchestral theme of An American in Paris just three months after its Carnegie Hall debut. Ira Gershwin MGM Movie Contract (December 27, 1949): A historic 6-page studio contract signed by the legendary lyricist for the Academy Award-winning MGM musical An American in Paris. The contract maps out his $56,250 pay structure and includes the famous studio "morals and conduct" clause used to keep contract players under the studio's thumb. John F. Kennedy & Robert Frost Inaugural Booklet (April 1961): A unique presentation copy of the limited-edition booklet printed for Robert Frost’s White House reception. It features Frost's dedication poem alongside the full text of JFK's historic "Ask not what your country can do for you" speech. It is signed by Kennedy on the cover and features a warm inscription from Frost to a journalist friend detailing the plane flight they shared. Ernest Hemingway Overseas Background Check (Undated): A jovial letter handwritten entirely in pencil to his hunting buddy Charles Thompson—the direct inspiration for "Karl" in The Green Hills of Africa. Hemingway requests that Thompson serve as a character witness for a government background check so he can travel overseas, writing with his signature wit: "If they interrogate you you can tell them what a good patriot, swell guy, always pay my debts (within two years or 20)..."Jerome Kern Signed Sheet Music (May 19, 1938): Vintage sheet music for the song "You Couldn't Be Cuter", inscribed to fellow film composer Lew Pollack. It is accompanied by a funny typed letter where Kern jokes that the song will probably be a "mummy by Decoration Day". Alex Haley Roots Inscription (June 25, 1984): A signed card featuring a good-natured sentiment referencing his ground-breaking saga, sending brotherly love from "Chicken George" and the family of Kunta Kinte. California Gold Rush Prospector Letter (July 25, 1849): A fascinating 3-page letter written by early 49er Mason R. Packer from Stockton, California, to his wife back east. Packer notes the exorbitant prices of basic goods in the boomtowns and coordinates his departure for the gold diggings near Sutter's Fort. The Honeymooners Cast Signed Photograph: A vintage publicity still showing the four core cast members (Jackie Gleason, Audrey Meadows, Art Carney, and Joyce Randolph) hanging out of a New York City bus window, signed beautifully by each actor. Charles Lindbergh Aviation Matte Portrait (Undated): A striking, oversized sepia waist-up portrait captured by Underwood & Underwood, showing Lindbergh standing proudly with the Spirit of St. Louis in the background, signed cleanly on the photographer's matte. Charles Lindbergh Leather Flight Portrait (Undated): A magnificent head-and-shoulders sepia portrait showing the youthful aviator clad in his complete leather flight jacket, helmet, and goggles, signed in bold black ink. Both Lindbergh portraits originated directly from the estate of the nation's very first federal aviation regulator, William P. MacCracken. The Little Rascals Vintage Signatures (1938–1939): A rare and highly desirable collector's set of five individual autograph leaves signed by the core childhood stars of the fabled Hal Roach Our Gang comedies, including Spanky McFarland, Buckwheat, Alfalfa, Darla Hood, and Porky Lee. Willie Mosconi Signed Billiard Ball Set: A complete presentation box containing fifteen individual billiard balls and an accompanying cue ball, each signed in full by the perennial 15-time world champion. The catalog notes his historic 1954 exhibition record where he sank an unbelievable 526 consecutive pool balls without a single miss. George S. Patton Cadet Letters (c. Fall 1903): A beautiful early letter written as a young cadet attending the Virginia Military Institute (VMI) to his aunt. Exhibiting his lifelong obsession with historical military tactics, the future general explicitly asks her to bring him white writing paper (rejecting blue paper as un-military) along with a newly published textbook entitled Strategy as Illustrated in British Campaigns. Richard Nixon Anti-Communist Speech (c. April 1953): A massive 15-page original typed speech layout containing extensive handwritten corrections and segregation notes by Vice President Richard Nixon. Plunging into a aggressive defense of his controversial role hunting down hidden Communists on the House Un-American Activities Committee (HUAC), Nixon defends the Alger Hiss investigations and prophetically maps out future international relations in East Asia. Roy Rogers & Gabby Hayes Signed Photo: A vintage 8x10 black-and-white publicity still showing both iconic Western screen stars in full costume, signed boldly across the image. Albert Schweitzer Aspen Visit (July 7, 1949): A striking portrait photograph of the philosopher and medical missionary, signed and dated during his historic summer visit to Aspen, Colorado. Piotr Ilyich Tchaikovsky Signed Cabinet Photo: An exceptional sepia vignette portrait photograph signed boldly across the image in Cyrillic script. The catalog hails this piece as perhaps the finest signed visual artifact of the legendary romantic composer in existence. Harriet Beecher Stowe Signed Quote: A crisp ink signature by the abolitionist author of Uncle Tom's Cabin, penning a biblical quote: "Trust in the Lord and do good." Booker T. Washington Tuskegee Appeal (January 27, 1894): A letter written on official school stationery to a New York judge. The iconic educator appeals for financial tuition sponsorships for poor but worthy Black students, written just one year prior to his historic "Atlanta Compromise" race-relations address. Mark Twain Faded Portrait (April 1909): A beautiful sepia-tone portrait showing the elderly humorist seated in a wooden chair, affectionately signed and inscribed: "Truly yours, Mark Twain. For Elizabeth."Elizabeth Taylor Nibbles and Me Hardcover (1946): A rare copy of the children's book written and illustrated entirely by a 13-year-old Elizabeth Taylor immediately following her breakout success in National Velvet. The book is warmly inscribed on the inside cover: "Lots of Love – From Nibbles & Elizabeth." Global Conflict & World War II Relics Erwin Rommel "Desert Fox" Postcard (September 9, 1939): A historic, mint-condition postcard handwritten in German by Rommel to his wife, Lucia Mollin, just eight days after the Nazi invasion of Poland sparked World War II. Rommel marvels at his new assignment commanding Hitler's guard battalion, writing with chilling confidence: "Things are going amazingly well for me... If we manage to maintain this pace, the war will be over in the West by the end of October, in my opinion." Admiral Chester Nimitz Propaganda handbill (February 1945): A wartime typed letter signed by Fleet Admiral Nimitz to an 1.1-year-old girl who shared his birthday. As a gift, Nimitz encloses an authentic U.S. propaganda bill dropped by Allied bombers over the Japanese mainland. The item is a 10-yen note printed on the back with a Japanese warning blasting the military cartel for wasting 5,000 yen per person on a losing war. Captured Okinawa "Rising Sun" Flag: An original silk Japanese military banner captured during the brutal Battle of Okinawa by a U.S. Army Major. The flag features printed margins translating to fierce nationalist slogans: "Our Military Strength Will Last Forever" and "Hoping for a Quick War." Gregory "Pappy" Boyington Flying Tigers Jacket: The authentic, black satin reversible flight jacket acquired directly from the estate of the legendary Marine Corps flying ace. The breast features embroidered stylized birds, the back showcases a fierce yellow tiger, and the reverse side maps out a detailed quilted green chart labeling major Japanese target cities around Mount Fuji. Charlie Owens D-Day Mapping Board (April 7, 1944): An original large perspective drawing accomplished in ink and pastel by the Los Angeles Times sketch artist. Dated exactly two months prior to the Allied invasion, the journalistic map utilizes sweeping arrows to project the exact troop movement paths that would be used on D-Day. Chaim Weizmann Palestine University Letter (July 10, 1903): A typed letter signed by the future first President of Israel, mapping out early zionist circulars to advocate for the foundation of a Jewish university in Palestine to combat academic discrimination in Europe.

results.title: ANYWHERE - 2 - a mediterranean trip
results.description: And so, as it goes, at this point, I may be somewhere on the border area between south Portugal and south Spain, slowly walking on the side of some kind of motorway going across a swamp sort of thing, now, watching the wader birds hopping through the ponds around, this is, probably migratory creatures coming from the other side of the strait, I mean, from Africa, and then, as I think about the p ossible trajectories these birds would do in order to get here, how they manage to n escape the Sahara winds etc, at some point, I would get a ride in a transporter, say, that kind of vans transporting furniture and home stuff from old addresses to new addresses. And well, as soon as I get in, Yan, the driver’s name, a middle aged guy with blond hair, goatee and sideburns, immediately says that he’s actually on the way to Gibraltar, plus, “after a small stop in Sevilla, I should be on the way to the south again” he adds, and, “oh, that suits me perfectly... that’s exactly where I wanna go!” I say, “Gibraltar?”, “yes, Gibraltar, Algeciras, and then Barcelona, France, Italy, Greece, Turkey, Egypt, and then north Africa, I mean, I wanna go all around the Mediterranean sea, and come back to Spain through Morocco!!”, “Oh,” he says, and then, “that seems tough!” he adds while showing some kind of intrigued smile, hence, thereupon, after we have actually passed Ayamonte, the first town in Spain, “actually I was born in the Balkans...” he says, “my mother was from there, just my father is English… this meaning that, well, I spent part of my childhood in different islands of the Aegean Sea… places like Lesbos, Chios, Samos, Naxos, and so on… and well, I also may say that… at some point, my best friends there, in this islands, were mainly the sons and the daughters of the A-zian refugees living on the campsites nearby…. and then, on my teens, well, I was sent to an auntie in Italy, and then, to another relative in France, and just then, I went to visit the old family in North Yorkshire, where I spent four or five year doing some schooling… that, before getting into a parade with a bunch of con hippies that would drive me away from Europe into Anatolian lands, I mean east Turkey, and then Iran, Afghanistan, Nepal, Laos, Vietnam… the Siam area, I mean Thailand, Malaysia and Singapore, and just then, from Indonesia into Australia we went… I mean, we would pass through many Indonesian islands, places like Java, Bali, Lombok, West Nusa Tenggara, East Nusa Tenggara, Timor and other smaller ones…'', he says, and “Uoou, whata big journey!” I would exclaim, and then, “What about Australia, how was it?” I ask, and he, “pretty boring... I mean, soon I would pass myself into New Zealand where people are more... yeah, once there, soon I would jump onto a big ship that would take me across the pacific ocean, South America, Chile, Argentina, Uruguay, Brazil, and then… the Caribbeans…”; “Ohu, looks amazing, I myself I have only been in Mexico… what about you, in which islands of Caribbeans have you been?” I would ask. And thus, while he talks about his experiences in the Caribbean islands, we would already be passing Jerez de la Frontera and then we would even take a shortcut through the Los Alcornocales Natural Park , where lays a typically Mediterranean forest, rich in oak and laurel trees, and so, while going through this park we would actually make some sudden stops at the houses(cottages) of certain expatriated friends of him, there isolated in the middle of nowhere, and so, what exactly happened there I can’t remember now, this is, I only recall that on the next morning I would see myself in front of the Algeciras port, and so, here I’m now, actually, not so far from the port, here sitting on the terrace of some Arab-style cafes run by ex-Moroccans, I mean, some of this beard guys actually have beaded necklaces in their hands, and while they shout, they drink and smoke, they also count the beads from their necklaces, and so, as it goes, I can understand some kind of French-Arab languages, and also some kind of Sanish-Arab languages, and then, as I get aware of a new guy that just came to seat on the table on my side, alone, a guy actually drinking beer, not shay, as all the others, and so, as he drinks, I wonder if he’s also an Arab like the others or an European like me, and so, as I try to unveil that, by looking at his attire, his style, at some point, he’s already questioning me “Yendo a Tanger!? Necesitas boletos!?“, this is, he’s actually asking me if I’m thinking of going to Tangier, and if I need t ickets, ferry tickets I presume. And thus, quickly, I got to know his name is Amir, a name that means “prince”, or “ruler” in his native language, and then, with a quaint smile on his face and a pinch of mockery on his voice, he’s already questioning, in Spanish again, “pero, veo que eres viajero, ahora, si no a Marruecos, ¿a dónde estás dispuesto a ir?” (but, I can see that you are some kind of traveler, I mean, if not to Morocco, where are you willing to go, afterall?) he says, and me, well, “I wanna go somewhere… but east, not south now…” I say. “Este, no sur” he repeats “like what, Jerusalem? Meca?” he asks, “Maybe!” I say. And then, as we speak about the differences between Jerusalem and Mecca, A mir is already pulling up a ready-made joint from behind his ear and inviting me to smoke with him. And then, as we leave the tables and go for a walk in front of the port, he’s actually telling me about his Mediterranean crossings and about his illegal stays in European lands all this time. So, as a start, he just tells me that he had crossed the Bāb al- M aghrib for the first time when he was still a teenager, “with a group of friends,” he says “I mean, we did it in a really small dinghy made out of inner tubes from truck wheels… but it happened that the sea dragged us too much to the west, and instead of landing on the Spanish coast, we ended up landing in south Portugal… what they call Algarve… and, with some luck, we weren't pulled into the Atlantic sea… but, as soon as we moored there, my friends quickly left to Spain, leaving me alone there, and so, I would wonder around Tavira, Lagos, Faro, etc… and then, actually, I would go up in the direction of the capital, Lisbon, where I would remain during some time, and well, I may say that… I liked the Portuguese people, they are humbler than the Spanish, but, there aren't great job opportunities in that country, so, after getting to know Almada, Sintra and Setubal, I would leave Portugal and go to work negro in the huge orange tree farms in south Spain, mainly located around Valencia, a city that have ferries to the famous island of Ibiza, and, well, at some point, I would actually manage to get into one of that ferries but, would get caught on the arrival and, they just sent me to some special kind of prison for illegals that turned out to be a nice house with some kind of labor camp, and it was there that I got to know and make friendship with other people from the Maghreb countries, like Algeria, Tunisia, Libya and some sub-sahariens also, people from Mali, Niger, Chad etc… and also, it was there, that I learned to properly speak and write Spanish, and then, some months later, when I was already integrated, they sent me back to Morocco… I mean, my mother was happy to see me again, but my older brother… as soon as I arrived he would throw me out of the house, this because, he would say, I had become an infidel, thus, I left again, this is, I wandered through the country and ended up not far from Ouarzazate, a touristic city at the doors of the desert, just on the side of the Barrage el Mansour Eddahbi , where I would work for a while, this before taking the caravan to Merzouga, a city on the border with Algeria…” and thus, as he says these things we are already walking, going along the sidewalk of Av. Virgen del Carmen , pass ing by Casa Pastor, a restaurant, and we also pass by the tapas bar El Cartuchito , the Estrella supermarket , the Locutorio Azizphone, the WesternUnion , the Moneygram offices , and we pass the Hispa-Maroc voyages , a travel agency, we pass Generali , an insurance office with many scooters parked in front of it, and we pass another Locutorio, another travel agency and then El Bazar Chino – Artículos de regalo , a gift shop, and the Kind Doner , a Pakistani fast food store, we pass the Adecco Staffing , a job agency, and then some kind of kiosk with a lot of shampoos on display, lottery cards and a big collection of peanut chocolate bars, etc. Then another supermarket named “ Alimentacion Rida ”, and on the side is the “ Golden Shawarma ” Indian restaurant, then the “ Turkish Kebab Pizza ”, and the “ Xavier Kadavid Peluqueros ”, a hairdresser, and the “ Farmacia Paseo Marítimo ”, and then we turn left and go up along the Calle Trafalgar and as we actually pass a shisha bar with arabesque doorways, Amir just comes back to his nomadic stories “lidha… entonces, somehow…” he says, “I found myself in Tunis, Tunisia's capital, where I would hear about a place where people could cross into Europe, the so called the Djerba peninsula , and so, there I went into some kind of dinghy due to Malta, this is, a European island I had never heard about… this is, an island where people can actually speak Arab, Italian and French, all mixed up… so, I liked it, and, in the meanwhile, I would even get a girlfriend there, this is, some months after, when I was already in Sic i lia, I would actually get to know that this girlfriend I had left behind, was actually pregnant… but, I couldn't go back, coz, now, I was working for the mafia, this is, I was a courier, I traveled between Sicily and another cities in south Italy a dozen times per month, cities like Napoli, Taranto, Lecce, Catanzaro, Bari, Brindisi, etc. And it happened that, at some point, I had to escape the mafia because they wanted to kill me, they said I was robbing them, and so… I went to France, it was my first time in France… I stayed mainly between Marseille and Montpelier, but got into a series of problems with some Algerian guys, who were the majority there, and, say, these Algerians were actually very different from the ones I had known in Algiers and other Algerian cities. Thus, it happened that, I would get into pitch battles with them, and so, in one of this brawls, the police just came by, I was arrested, they found out that I was illegal and I was sent back to my country… so, this is, on the arrival, my mother was happy again, but not my brothers… same old shit… and, in the meanwhile, I would get to know that one of my girlfriends in France was actually pregnant, again, and so, again, I wo uld find a way to cross the bahar …”, he says as we go along “Calle Pablo Mayayo”, now passing the headquarters of the “ El Faro ” newspaper, then, we turn right, we pass the “ Bar la Esquina ” and we arrive at the “ Plaza Alta ”, an open square with some high palm trees, a fountain in the middle, and a couple circular benches around, benches decorated with the Seville style tiles, this is, matted patterns with strong blue and strong yellow, and on the opposite side, on other benches, there are some elders talking loud and hoarse, and looking the sky from time to time. And so, while they look the sky, Amir continues his story, “I came back to France in order to marry that woman that was pregnant, so I could get the European papers, but it happened that she didn't want to marry me, coz her family was Algerin, and no Algerian woman should marry a Moroccan man… therefore, I left again, I went to German and to Switzerland but I couldn't adapt to the coldness, so, I decided to come back to Italy, and again, I ended up in Sicily, thinking about crossing to Malta and look for my other child, but, I was caught, one the mafia guys recognized me and I actually passed some bad times in their hands before I manage to escape… so, this time, I went to Libya, found some serious work in Tripoli, this is, I even shook hands with one of the sons of Qaddafi...” and, as he say those things, we are now going along “ Playa de El Rinconcillo ”, from where we can already see the Gibraltar peninsula, and so, with one foot on the sand and other one on the gravel we smoked that thing in silence, and then, I wanted to keep my journey, so, Amir accompanied me until the city exit, this is, we go by the motorway until reaching a bridge over the “ Palmones River ”, and, on the other side of this bridge there would be a big roundabout, and so, it was there, on this roundabout, that we would separate. Then, quickly, I would get a ride with some dentist guy coming from Seville, this is, he just went there to pick up some prostheses for his consultor io in Marbella. Ayesha was educated at the Paris Diderot University, and studied law at the Sorbonne. She trained with the Libyan military, reaching the rank of lieutenant colonel. In 2000 after sanctions were imposed on Iraq, she arrived in Baghdad with a delegation of 69 officials, and shortly before the invasion of Iraq, she met with Saddam Hussein… later she would sued NATO over the bombing of a building in her father's compound which she alleged killed her brother, Saif al-Arab Qaddafi, and her own infant daughter. Later, during the revolution, along with two of her brothers and other family members, she left Algeria to go to Oman, where other members of the Q addaf i family are currently living…”. And so, now, as we get out in the port of Algiers, I cross the Rampe Magenta and enter a piazza garden with some small palm trees and a bandstand in the middle, a nouvelle vague bandstand like the ones I have seen in some gardens in Lisbon. And they tell me this is the Port Saïd Square. Then I go along the Abane Ramdane street, there is a huge building on my right with a series of arches and on my left I see a store named Miss Dunya Lissa, a clothes shop with some old fashioned pajamas for women, slightly risky necklines, lacy sleeves, like the female nightwear of the 80s, then a couple of shops with home goods like towels, bedspreads, aprons, trench coats, toilet brushes, etc, then I pass the Hotel Akfado, a couple of boutiques more, raw perfumes stores, the Motel Odeon capsules, the Redouan Episse, that is selling packaged spices and some different kinds of roots, and I arrive at an archaeological excavation site, named Quartier Ottoman de la Basse Casbah. I keep going through the lane Bab El Oued, I pass some carpet stores and I arrive at the Martyrs' Square, a square with some more palm trees and a couple of minarets in the back. Then I turn left and I go up through a series of narrow staircases, and at some point, I arrive at the Palais Dar Ahmed Pasha, this is, from here I can see the coast and the sea, and the Dar Mustapha Pacha and the Dar Souf Palace. Then I go through the Rue de l'Indépendance and I arrive at the Rue du Diable, which is a staircase inside a tunnel, and on the top of it there is an old man, seated on the balustrade, he greets me, I greet him and we act out a conversation. I ask him why this alley is named “devil street” and he tells me about Barbarossa, the famous pirate of the “albahr al'abyad almutawasit”, the mediterranean sea. He tells me that he used to come here into these alleys, looking for girls. “Originally named Khayr al-Din Barbarus , also known as Hayreddin Pasha, romanticized Barbarossa by the Italians...” he tells me in french language, . “was an Ottoman corsair and later admiral of the Ottoman Navy, by Suleiman the Magnificent, that great pasha famous for the Siege of Vienna.… Barbarossa was actually born in Lesbos, the Greek/Turkish island on the aegean sea, and began his naval career as a corsair under his elder brother Oruç Reis, that captured Algiers from Spain, then following Oruç's death, Khayr inherited his brother's achievements and became one of the most feared man in the Mediterranean… he captures Tunis, Gibraltar, Sicil y and some other Greek islands…” and then, after saying this things, the old man stands up and makes me signal to accompany him, and so, he takes me precisely to the Barbarous street, which is just some alleys up, and from there we enter another alley named Rue Kataroudjil and in some minutes we debouch at a kind of natural balcony, from where we can see all the Bay of Algiers. Next morning I come back to the port and I manage to board another small ship that goes in the direction of the Morocco coast. Apparently the ship is carrying a cargo of detergents, things made in China, that were exported to Libya, but Libya discarded them to Tunisia, and Tunisia discarded it to Algeria, and now, Algeria is passing it to Morocco. And so, as we go along the M oroccan coast, we pass cities like Saidia, Nador,  Al Hoceima, El Jebha, and then, Tétouan and Tangier, where I disembark, and then, there I go, in the direction of Cape Spartel, where is the Spartel Bank, a sunken island hypothesized by some as being the location of the legendary Atlantis islan d.

results.title: Don Quijote
results.creator: Lars52719
results.description: Miguel de Cervantes Saavedra (Alcalá de Henares,​ 29 de septiembre de 1547-Madrid, 22 de abril​ de 1616) fue un novelista, poeta, dramaturgo y soldado español. Es ampliamente considerado una de las máximas figuras de la literatura española. Fue el autor de El ingenioso hidalgo don Quijote de la Mancha, novela conocida habitualmente como El Quijote, que lo llevó a ser mundialmente conocido y a la cual muchos críticos han descrito como la primera novela moderna, así como una de las mejores obras de la literatura universal, cuya cantidad de ediciones y traducciones solo es superada por la Biblia.​ A Cervantes se le ha dado el apelativo de «Príncipe de los Ingenios» Infancia y juventud Torre de la iglesia de Santa María la Mayor de Alcalá de Henares, donde bautizaron a Miguel de Cervantes. Resultó destruida en un incendio durante la guerra civil española.Desde el siglo XVIII está admitido que el lugar de nacimiento de Miguel de Cervantes fue Alcalá de Henares,4​ dado que allí fue bautizado, según su acta bautismal, y que de allí aclaró ser natural en la llamada Información de Argel (1580).

results.title: ERIC ED046274: Cautivos Precervantinos, Cara y Cruz del Cautiverio (Pre-Cervantine Captives and the Condition of Their Captivity).
results.creator: ERIC
results.description: Miguel de Cervantes' capture by the Turks and his imprisonment in Argel (Morocco) during the Battle of Lepanto in the sixteenth century have been studied by literary critics who have endeavored to determine fiction and reality in certain episodes of "Don Quijote" and in the drama, "Los banos de Argel". Twelve documents published here provide background data on Spanish prisoners held captive in Tetuan, Argel, and Velez. From the testimony presented and the similarities suggested, it is apparent that Cervantes drew his inspiration from real life experience. The linguistic, lexical, and idiomatic aspects of the documents are scrutinized to understand Cervantes' aesthetics. An abundance of information is offered on the prisoners including their dress, manners, speech, manner of capture, and the desolation, anguish and misery experienced. results.title: A torch kept lit : great lives of the twentieth century
results.creator: Buckley, William F., Jr., 1925-2008, author
description: 323 pages : 22 cm

"A unique collection of eulogies of the twentieth century's greatest figures, written by conservative icon William F. Buckley Jr. and compiled by National Review and Fox News chief Washington correspondent James Rosen. In a half-century on the national stage, William F. Buckley Jr. achieved unique stature as a polemicist and the undisputed godfather of modern American conservatism. He knew everybody, hosted everybody at his East 73rd Street maisonette, skewered everybody who needed skewering, and in general lived life on a scale, and in a swashbuckling manner, that captivated and inspired countless young conservatives across that half-century. Among all of his distinctions, which include founding the conservative magazine National Review and serving as host on the long running talk show Firing Line, Buckley was a master of that most elusive of art forms: the eulogy. Buckley drew on his unrivaled gifts in what he liked to call 'the controversial arts' to mourn, celebrate, or seek eternal mercy for the men and women who touched his life and the nation; to conjure their personalities, recall memorable moments, herald their greatness; or to remind readers of why a given individual, even with the grace that death can uniquely confer, should be remembered as evil. At all points, these remembrances reflect Buckley's singular voice, with its elegant touch and mordant humor, and lend to the lives of the departed a final tribute consistent with their own careers, lives, and accomplishments. Of the more than 200 eulogies located in Buckley's vast archive of published works, A Torch Kept Lit collects the very best, those remembering the most consequential lives (Kennedy, Nixon, Reagan), the most famous to today's readers (Elvis Presley, John Lennon, Jacqueline Onassis, Princess Diana), those who loomed largest in the conservative movement (Milton Friedman, Russell Kirk), the most accomplished in the literary world (Norman Mailer, Truman Capote, William Shawn), the most mysterious (Soviet spy Alger Hiss, CIA spymaster Richard Helms), and those most dear to WFB (his wife and parents)"--

From Wikipedia; The American Magazine  was a  periodical publication  founded in June 1906, a continuation of failed publications purchased a few years earlier from publishing mogul  Miriam Leslie . It succeeded  Frank Leslie's Popular Monthly  (1876–1904),  Leslie's Monthly Magazine  (1904–1905),  Leslie's Magazine  (1905) and the  American Illustrated Magazine  (1905–1906). [ 1 ]  The magazine was published through August 1956. History [ edit ] Under the magazine's original title,  Frank Leslie's Popular Monthly , it had begun to be published in 1876 and was renamed  Leslie's Monthly Magazine  in 1904, and then was renamed again as  Leslie's Magazine  in 1905. [ 2 ]  From September 1905, through May 1906, it was entitled the  American Illustrated Magazine ; then subsequently shortened as  The American Magazine  until publication ceased in 1956. It kept continuous volume numbering throughout its history. [ 2 ] In June 1906,  muckraking   journalists   Ray Stannard Baker ,  Lincoln Steffens  and  Ida M. Tarbell  left  McClure's  to help create  The American Magazine . An "Editorial Announcement" published in 1907 led with Tarbell's coverage of tariff policy. [ 3 ]  Baker contributed articles using the pseudonym  David Grayson . Under  John Sanborn Phillips , who served as editor until 1915, the monthly magazine departed somewhat from the muckraking style and focused on human interest stories, social issues and fiction. Initially published by his Phillips Publishing Company of  Springfield ,  Ohio , it later was taken over by Crowell Publishing Company in 1911, [ 4 ]  and later merged with  Collier's .  The American Magazine  was published by  Crowell-Collier  until it folded in 1956. [ 5 ] Editors [ edit ] With the changes in 1915, John M. Siddall (1915–23) was appointed as editor of the periodical, which expanded its market considerably by concentrating on a female readership. The cover of the September 1917 issue announced: "This Magazine's Circulation Has Doubled in 20 Months." The September 1922 cover stated circulation had reached 1.8 million. Merle Crowell served as editor of  The American Magazine  from 1923 until 1929 when  Sumner Blossom  took over. Blossom, who had been editor of  Popular Science , was there for the last 27 years of the magazine's existence. Fictional  serials  and  short stories  were a popular feature, and the magazine published several winners of the  O. Henry Awards . High-profile writers contributed articles on a variety of topics. During his editorship, Blossom adopted the policy of hiding the author's name on all works of fiction during the selection process as a way to encourage new fiction writers. The magazine's staff learned the author's identity only once they accepted or rejected a manuscript. The last issue of  The American Magazine  was displayed on newsstands in August 1956. [ 6 ] Stories [ edit ] In 1934,  The American Magazine  ran a story called "Uncle Sam Grows Younger" that praised  Alger Hiss : "In his twenties, he is one of the men chiefly responsible for the plan to buy $650,000,000 worth of commodities to feed the unemployed. results.title: A torch kept lit : great lives of the twentieth century
results.creator: Buckley, William F., Jr., 1925-2008, author
description: 323 pages : 22 cm

"A unique collection of eulogies of the twentieth century's greatest figures, written by conservative icon William F. Buckley Jr. and compiled by National Review and Fox News chief Washington correspondent James Rosen. In a half-century on the national stage, William F. Buckley Jr. achieved unique stature as a polemicist and the undisputed godfather of modern American conservatism. He knew everybody, hosted everybody at his East 73rd Street maisonette, skewered everybody who needed skewering, and in general lived life on a scale, and in a swashbuckling manner, that captivated and inspired countless young conservatives across that half-century. Among all of his distinctions, which include founding the conservative magazine National Review and serving as host on the long running talk show Firing Line, Buckley was a master of that most elusive of art forms: the eulogy. Buckley drew on his unrivaled gifts in what he liked to call 'the controversial arts' to mourn, celebrate, or seek eternal mercy for the men and women who touched his life and the nation; to conjure their personalities, recall memorable moments, herald their greatness; or to remind readers of why a given individual, even with the grace that death can uniquely confer, should be remembered as evil. At all points, these remembrances reflect Buckley's singular voice, with its elegant touch and mordant humor, and lend to the lives of the departed a final tribute consistent with their own careers, lives, and accomplishments. Of the more than 200 eulogies located in Buckley's vast archive of published works, A Torch Kept Lit collects the very best, those remembering the most consequential lives (Kennedy, Nixon, Reagan), the most famous to today's readers (Elvis Presley, John Lennon, Jacqueline Onassis, Princess Diana), those who loomed largest in the conservative movement (Milton Friedman, Russell Kirk), the most accomplished in the literary world (Norman Mailer, Truman Capote, William Shawn), the most mysterious (Soviet spy Alger Hiss, CIA spymaster Richard Helms), and those most dear to WFB (his wife and parents)"--

results.title: The Secret History of the Atomic Bomb - Eustace Mullins
results.description: Los alemanes y los japoneses estaban investigando sobre la fisión nuclear desde los años 30.   En el año 1939, los judíos húngaros Edward Teller, Leo Szilard y Eugene Winger huyen de su país y se integran en el selecto comité estadounidense coordinado por el también judío exiliado Albert Einstein que pretende lograr la bomba atómica antes que los alemanes (y utilizarla).   La composición de dicho comité, que más tarde se convertirá en el Comité de la Energía Atómica, es fundamental para conocer quién dio la orden de detonarla: otro judío, Robert Oppenheimer, perteneciente a la familia de comerciantes de diamantes, está al mando científico. Cuando el secretario de guerra Stimson le habla al General Eisenhower de la existencia de la bomba, el popular Ike se entristeció enormemente y negó la necesidad de golpear a Japón con la nueva arma. Tres días después, se va a Berlín a intentar convencer al presidente Truman de que no la lancen. Truman, por cierto, había llegado al poder tras la repentina y SOSPECHOSÍSIMA muerte de Roosvelt, y su único empleo conocido era ser el jefe de las logias masónicas de Missouri. Stimson pertenecía a los Skull and Bones de la Universidad de Yale. Contrariamente a lo que nos han hecho creer, Einstein detestaba los derechos humanos y en intercambio epistolar con Freud, se reía de sus convicciones pacifistas. El 2 de agosto de 1939, el “pacifista” Einstein envió una carta a Roosevelt a través del agente Sachs animándole a trabajar en el proyecto de bomba atómica. El tal Sachs era asesor de los hermanos banqueros judíos Lazard y Lehman, y fundó la hoy conocidísima Goldman Sachs. En mayo de 1945, mientras Hitler se está rindiendo (y escapando gracias a la ayuda de los sionistas) rumbo a Argentina, los aliados ponen en marcha la ONU en el Hotel Palace de San Francisco. Un pequeñísimo grupo se reúne en un jardín para terminar los estatutos de la hoy conocida organización: el abogado de Wall Street John Foster Dulles (su hermano fue el primer jefe de la CIA), el representante de Estados Unidos Alger Hiss, el revolucionario a sueldo de Wall Street William Nelson Cromwell, el banquero Avery Harriman, que ha pasado los dos últimos años ayudando a Stalin en Moscú (representando a la URSS) y el secretario de estado USA Sttetinus, hijo del socio del banquero J.P. Morgan. Este último les emplaza para hablar del lanzamiento de la bomba atómica sobre Japón. La conversación se desarrolla en los términos de saber cómo justificar el empleo de dicha bomba si, con la capitulación de Alemania y los llamamientos a la paz del Emperador Hirohito, la guerra está prácticamente terminada. Entonces, Foster Dulles dice: “Keep Japan in the war another three months, and we can use the bomb on their cities; we will end this war with the naked fear of all the peoples of the world, who will then bow to our will.”   Es decir: “mantened a Japón en la guerra otros tres meses, y podremos usar la bomba sobre sus ciudades: acabaremos la guerra con el miedo desnudo de las gentes del mundo y los tendremos a nuestros pies”. Lanzar la bomba atómica era vital para lanzar la guerra fría, que mantendría a la Humanidad sometida ante el miedo a la destrucción durante la segunda mitad del siglo XX: antes de acabar la II Guerra Mundial ya comenzaron esta nueva guerra. Para lo cual, obviamente, los propios banqueros capitalistas pasaron a los soviéticos el secreto de la bomba atómica, a través de “Los cinco de Cambridge” entre los que estaba el barón Rothschild y el escritor Ian Fleming (James Bond). Entre el grupo que decidió lanzar la bomba, además, había tres políticos/banqueros comunistas que aconsejaban a la Unión Soviética: Hiss, Cromwell y Harriman. El hecho de que todo esto sucediera en mayo de 1945, para mí es la prueba insoslayable de que el acuerdo para que Hitler escapara fue, como dice Abel Basti, entregarle el secreto de la bomba atómica a Estados Unidos. Una bomba que el desalmado Hitler se habría negado a utilizar por razones de conciencia. (Los dirigentes actuales del mundo, en cambio, no). Es fácil saber quién hizo ese pacto, pues el hermano de Foster Dulles, Allan, jefe de la empresa farmacéutica alemana Farben, hombre de Kuhn and Loeb y Rothschild, ayudó a financiar el partido Na-Zionista alemán. El Proyecto de la bomba atómica es judío desde el inicio. La persona responsable, Bernard Baruch, vivía en Manhattan, de ahí que a ese proyecto secreto se le diera el nombre de “Proyecto Manhattan”. También pertenecían al consejo asesor sobre defensa, el presidente de la Universidad de Harvard, Conant (impulsor del anthrax) y el presidente de la Reserva Federal de Nueva York, George L. Harrison. El judío lituano Lipman Siew que se cambió el nombre por el de William L. Laurence   y escribía en el New York Times, otro hombre de Baruch, supervisó el proyecto como “relaciones públicas” de un proyecto totalmente secreto. (!!).   Él fue el único civil que pudo ver el test de la bomba atómica en Los Alamos, Nuevo Méjico, y quien se sentó en el asiento del copiloto en el nefasto avión Enola Gay, que lanzó la bomba atómica. De las 66 ciudades más grandes del Japón, 59 habían sido casi completamente destruidas en marzo de 1945. Sólo unas pocas se habían salvado de los ataques, entre ellas Kokura, Niigata, Hiroshima y Nagasaki. La razón es que querían que estuvieran indemnes para así poder comprobar la potencia de la bomba atómica. Baruch, a través del General Groves, quería lanzarla sobre Kioto, pero el hecho de que tuviera un gran número de templos nipones hizo que desestimaran esta opción. Aunque Truman se atribuya la autoría del lanzamiento, su total inexperiencia en el campo de las relaciones internacionales hizo que estuviera bajo el control del hombre de Baruch, James F. Byrnes. La bomba atómica abrió una nueva etapa para la Humanidad, al conocer que un invento del ser humano era capaz de acabar con la vida en el Planeta. El propio Oppenheimer explicó que aquel día era “el agente de la muerte y la destrucción”.   La barbarie y la humanidad alcanzaron su mayor grado aquel día (y seguramente se inventaron lo del holocausto para ocultarlo) y fueron los ganadores del conflicto que lo llevaron a cabo. Su objetivo, según revela el libro de Mullins repleto de citas, era conducir a la Humanidad al miedo total. Una de las mentiras que nos contaron es que lanzaron panfletos sobre Hiroshima avisando al pueblo: la realidad es que los lanzaron varios días después de la masacre. El 1 de junio de 1945, Oppenheimer y Byrnes habían decidido que las bombas debían lanzarse sin avisar previamente a la gente. Otra creencia errónea es que ambas ciudades eran blancos militares. La realidad es que en Hiroshima había 20.000 soldados (la mitad murieron) y en Nagasaki murieron 150 militares. Es decir, el 4% de los fallecidos. Mientras tanto, el mencionado Lawrence/Lipman escribía en el New York Times a sueldo del ministerio de Defensa negando que hubiera víctimas por radiaciones. La noticia de que Hiroshima y Nagasaki habían sido destruidas se celebró entre alborozo por los científicos del Proyecto Manhattan, con Oppenheimer a la cabeza. Si alguna vez os habéis preguntado a qué se refieren las películas cuando hablan de científicos locos, esta es la respuesta. PD: Sólo son 17 páginas en inglés (el resto son citas). Este libro fue quemado en los años 60 por orden de uno de estos banqueros. No quieren que sepas la Verdad.
